# Team 26126 · Model explanation for the video

Nov 10, 2026 · @Sujal

## The big picture

A socket fits the child's arm on the day it is made, but the child keeps growing. Our answer has two parts. For a boy fitted at 8, a socket must be **replaced** about 17–22 months after fitting. And in our baseline, around **age 14** (earlier for bigger children), refitting stops working and the socket **design** must change. That second age is soft: it moves by several years when we change our assumptions (see "How firm is that age?" below).

**The question in our words.** A child with a below-elbow (transradial) prosthesis lifts objects. The socket is the cup that joins the prosthesis to the child's forearm. How do the forces between arm and socket change as the child grows, and when does that change become serious enough to need closer attention?

**How we built the answer.** We climbed a ladder of models, each one checked against the one below it:

1. **Growth model:** how tall and heavy the child is at each age (a differential equation fitted to CDC data).
2. **Model 0 (static):** the arm holds an object still. Pure free-body diagram, solved by hand.
3. **Model 1 (dynamic):** the arm lifts the object. Lagrange equations of a two-link arm.
4. **Model 2 (growth coupling):** the socket stays the same size while the arm grows. Two ways the fit can fail.
5. **Policy:** when to replace, how to save sockets, and the point of substantial change.
6. **Model 3 (extension):** what an outgrown prosthesis does to the trunk and joints.
7. **Verification and uncertainty:** tests that prove the maths, and 400 random parameter sets.

**The one sentence to remember:** socket pressure is a moment divided by the engaged length squared, and growth changes both.

## The child's arm

The residual limb grows fatter much faster than it grows longer, because the growth plates that make the forearm longer are missing.

**The parts, from shoulder to hand:**

| Part          | What it is                                      | In our model                          |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Upper arm     | the child's own humerus, shoulder to elbow      | link 1 of the arm, length 0.186 H     |
| Elbow         | the child's own joint; it drives the prosthesis | joint angle q2                        |
| Residual limb | what remains of the forearm below the elbow     | 45 % of the forearm length at fitting |
| Socket        | rigid cup moulded around the residual limb      | fixed size after fitting              |
| Prosthesis    | forearm shell + terminal device (hand or hook)  | 0.40 kg, ends at the grip point       |

**Why growth plates matter.** Long bones grow at growth plates (physes) near each end. In the forearm, the plates at the **wrist end** supply about 80 % (radius) and 85 % (ulna) of the length growth, more in mid-childhood (Pritchett 1991). A child born without the lower forearm, or who lost it early, has no wrist-end plates. So the residual limb gains only a small share of normal forearm length growth (we use **25 %**, a little above the 5–20 % those numbers suggest), while its **girth** keeps growing with the whole body.

That single fact explains most of our results: the socket problem is mainly about **girth**, not length.

**Words to use in the video:** transradial = below the elbow; residual limb = the remaining forearm; socket = the cup; terminal device = the hand or hook at the end.

## Growth model

Height follows the Preece–Baines growth ODE, which matches the official CDC median heights to 0.28 cm on average.

\\frac{dH}{dt} = s(t)\\,\\bigl(h_1 - H\\bigr), \\qquad s(t) = \\frac{s_0 e^{s_0(t-\\theta)} + s_1 e^{s_1(t-\\theta)}}{e^{s_0(t-\\theta)} + e^{s_1(t-\\theta)}}

**How to explain it.** H is height and h1 is adult height. The growth rate is proportional to how far the child still has to grow. The rate factor s(t) switches smoothly from a slow childhood value s0 to a fast puberty value s1 around age θ. That switch is the growth spurt.

| Fitted value         | Boys                | Girls               |
| -------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------- |
| Adult height h1      | 176.7 cm            | 163.1 cm            |
| Spurt age θ          | 14.0 y              | 12.3 y              |
| Peak growth velocity | 7.5 cm/yr at 13.4 y | 6.8 cm/yr at 11.6 y |
| Fit error (RMS)      | 0.28 cm             | 0.28 cm             |

**Girth.** We treat the forearm as a cylinder of tissue. Its mass grows with body mass M and its length with height H, so its radius grows like the square root of M/H:

r = \\sqrt{\\frac{m_f}{\\pi \\rho\\, \\ell_f}} \\;\\propto\\; \\sqrt{M/H}

**Data source.** CDC 2000 growth reference, LMS tables for stature and weight. The same tables give 10th and 90th centile children, so we can model small and large children too.

**Picture for the video:** fig01_growth (height vs data, growth velocity, limb radius).

## Model 0: the static socket

Holding an object still, a boy fitted at age 8 feels about 37 kPa of socket pressure from the load, and that pressure scales as the moment divided by the engaged length squared.

![Model 0 free-body diagram · forearm horizontal, object held still](data:image/png;base64,)

Model 0 free-body diagram · forearm horizontal, object held still

The weights of the prosthesis and object try to rotate the prosthesis downward. The socket stops that by pressing on the limb in two places: **up on the underside near the brim** and **down on the top near the distal end**. With the palm up, these are the back of the forearm near the elbow and the front near the end.

**Step 1: what the limb must hold.** A shear force V and a moment M about the socket brim:

V = g\\,(m_p + m_o), \\qquad M_B = g\\,(m_p x_p + m_o L_p)

**Step 2: spread it along the socket.** Assume the line load q(z) varies linearly along the engaged length L. Force balance and moment balance give the two edge values:

q(0) = \\frac{4V}{L} - \\frac{6M_B}{L^2}, \\qquad q(L) = -\\frac{2V}{L} + \\frac{6M_B}{L^2}

**Step 3: turn it into pressure.** Spread over half the circumference of a limb of radius r:

p_{mom} = \\frac{2\\max\\{|q(0)|,|q(L)|\\}}{\\pi r} \\;\\approx\\; \\frac{12\\,M_B}{\\pi r L^2}

**Scaling laws (the key insight).** For a new socket at each age, L grows with height H and r grows like the square root of M/H, so r·L grows like the square root of M·H.

- Same 0.5 kg object at every age: pressure falls as (MH) to the power −1/2. A bigger child copes better with the same bottle.
- Object that grows with the child (2 % of body mass): that part rises as (M/H) to the power +1/2.
- The code confirms both exponents exactly: −0.500 and +0.500.

**Pictures for the video:** this free-body diagram, then fig02_static_model.

## Model 1: lifting dynamics

Lifting fast raises socket pressure by almost 80 %: 77 kPa for a fast curl against 43 kPa for holding the same 0.5 kg object still.

**The four actions** (all in one plane, shoulder fixed, 0.5 kg object, boy fitted at 8):

| Action        | Shoulder   | Elbow      | Time  | Peak pressure |
| ------------- | ---------- | ---------- | ----- | ------------- |
| Static hold   | 0°         | 90°        | 1.0 s | 43.0 kPa      |
| Slow curl     | 5° → 20°   | 10° → 130° | 1.2 s | 43.3 kPa      |
| Lift to shelf | 10° → 100° | 30°        | 1.2 s | 48.1 kPa      |
| Fast curl     | 5° → 20°   | 10° → 130° | 0.5 s | 76.7 kPa      |

**How each joint moves.** Every joint follows a minimum-jerk path, the smoothest way to go from start to end angle. Real human reaching movements look like this.

q(\\tau) = q_0 + \\Delta q\\,(10\\tau^3 - 15\\tau^4 + 6\\tau^5), \\qquad \\tau = t/T

**Equations of motion.** The arm is two rigid links: the upper arm (link 1) and the residual limb, prosthesis and object together (link 2). Angle q1 is the shoulder, measured from hanging straight down; q2 is the elbow bend. Lagrange's method gives:

\\mathbf{M}(q_2)\\,\\ddot{\\mathbf{q}} + \\mathbf{C}(\\mathbf{q},\\dot{\\mathbf{q}}) + \\mathbf{G}(\\mathbf{q}) = \\boldsymbol{\\tau}

M is the mass matrix (inertia), C holds the Coriolis and centrifugal terms, G is gravity, and τ is the joint torques. We know the motion, so we solve for the torques (inverse dynamics). Then Newton–Euler on the prosthesis alone gives the force and moment the socket carries, which Model 0's formulas turn into pressure.

**The dimensionless number Π.** It compares the inertial moment with the gravity moment:

\\Pi = \\frac{10}{\\sqrt{3}}\\,\\frac{\\Delta q\\, L_p}{g\\,T^2}

We ran both curls for 8 children at 6 speeds, 96 runs in all. A straight line fits them closely: **pressure amplification ≈ 0.64 + 1.00 Π** (R² = 0.998). The slope is close to 1, which is what you would expect from a number that compares inertial and gravity load. Be careful with the 0.64: it belongs to the line, not to the physics. For slow curls (Π below about 0.3, 22 of the 96 runs) the amplification is 0.99–1.02, so a slow curl loads the socket just like holding still. The real curve is flat near 1 and then rises roughly one for one with Π. The line misses that flat start by up to 0.3, which is why we say: **below Π ≈ 0.3 speed barely matters; above it, load grows about linearly with Δq/T².**

**Pictures for the video:** fig03_actions, anim_fast_curl.gif, fig04_task_loads, fig05_dynamic_collapse.

## Model 2: the socket meets a growing arm

A socket fitted at age 8 lasts 21.6 months if it is cylindrical and 16.7 months if it is tapered. Across fitting ages 5–12 the model gives 13.5 to 37 months. We have not checked these against clinic data.

![Model 2 · the two interface mechanisms, boy fitted at age 8](data:image/png;base64,)

Model 2 · the two interface mechanisms, boy fitted at age 8

**What changes after fitting.** The socket is frozen; the limb is not.

\\ell_r(t) = \\ell_r(t_f) + 0.25\\,\[\\ell_f(t) - \\ell_f(t_f)\], \\qquad \\varepsilon(t) = \\frac{r(t) - r_s}{0.4\\, r(t)}, \\qquad p_{fit} = \\frac{E}{B}\\bigl(e^{B\\varepsilon} - 1\\bigr)

The residual length grows at 25 % of the forearm rate. The tissue strain ε grows as the radius r outgrows the socket radius r_s. Soft tissue stiffens as it is squeezed, so the fit pressure rises exponentially.

**Socket Stress Index.** Total peak pressure = fit pressure + lifting pressure from Model 1. We divide by the tolerance (100 kPa): SSI = p_peak / p_tol. A socket is replaced when SSI reaches 1.

**Two mechanisms, two failures:**

- **Cylindrical socket.** Growth squeezes the tissue. On day one, lifting causes 92 % of the pressure; at failure, the squeeze causes 39 %.
- **Tapered socket.** When the squeeze exceeds what the child can push against while putting it on (60 N), the limb sits out of the socket. That relieves the squeeze but shortens the engaged length from 84 mm to 75 mm (12 mm of ride-up). Since lifting pressure scales with 1/L squared, lifting takes over.

A real socket probably behaves somewhere between these two, but we haven't tested that.

**Pictures for the video:** this diagram, then fig06_single_socket and fig07_lifetime_map.

## The point of substantial change

When everyday loads grow with the child, then in our baseline, at 13.9 years for boys and 14.6 for girls, even a brand-new socket cannot stay under the pressure tolerance; from then on the socket design must change, not just its size. The exact ages depend on our assumptions (see below).

**Two kinds of change.** The problem asks for a point of substantial change. We found two, and the difference between them is the heart of our answer:

|              | Routine replacement                  | Window closure                                   |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| What happens | this socket is outgrown              | no socket of this design can cope                |
| When         | 17–22 months after fitting (boy fitted at 8) | about age 14 in our baseline (median child) |
| Fix          | make a new socket of the same design | redesign: longer socket, new suspension, harness |
| Cause        | girth squeeze or ride-up             | object term rising as (M/H)^½ from Model 0       |

**Why the window closes.** Model 0 showed the pressure of a new socket has two parts. The prosthesis part falls as the child grows. The object part rises if objects grow with the child (we assume 2 % of body mass). Once the rising part plus the minimum fit pressure reaches the tolerance, refitting cannot help.

**It depends on the child's size:**

| Child                 | Boys   | Girls         |
| --------------------- | ------ | ------------- |
| 10th centile (small)  | 16.2 y | not before 18 |
| 50th centile (median) | 13.9 y | 14.6 y        |
| 90th centile (large)  | 11.8 y | 11.4 y        |

Large children reach closure 2–3 years earlier, so screening should be triggered by **body size and residual-limb length**, not by age alone.

**How firm is that age?** Not very, and you should say so. We changed one assumption at a time (picture: fig14_closure_sensitivity):

| Change                                       | Boys                 | Girls                |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------- |
| baseline (object 2 % of body mass, 100 kPa)  | 13.9 y               | 14.6 y               |
| object 2.5 % of body mass                    | 10.4 y               | 10.1 y               |
| object 3 % of body mass                      | 7.0 y                | 7.2 y                |
| object 1.5 % of body mass                    | no closure before 18 | no closure before 18 |
| tolerance 75 kPa                             | 7.7 y                | 7.8 y                |
| tolerance 125 kPa                            | no closure before 18 | no closure before 18 |
| limb follows the 25 % growth rule from age 8 | 11.6 y               | 11.3 y               |
| prosthesis mass grows with height            | 13.3 y               | 13.3 y               |
| without the fast curl                        | no closure before 18 | no closure before 18 |

Two more things to know. Only the fast curl sets the closure age. And we found an inconsistency in our own baseline: each new socket is designed for a limb that is 45 % of the forearm at the age it is fitted, which makes the limb longer at 14 than our 25 % growth rule would allow. In the Monte Carlo runs 14 % of samples were already closed at age 4, 33 % never closed before 18, and only about 11 % landed within a year of 13.9. What we trust is the mechanism, not the number.

**A cheaper replacement policy.** Instead of the standard 5 % tissue squeeze, fit each socket at the loosest strain that still holds the prosthesis on, with a safety factor of 1.25. This growth allowance cuts a median boy's sockets from age 6 to 18 from **6 to 5**. For the median girl it stays at 5. In a remote area, that is one fewer fabrication and one fewer long journey to the clinic.

**Pictures for the video:** fig09_window_closure (the key slide), fig08_replacement_schedule.

## Model 3: the rest of the body

If a socket fitted at 8 is never replaced, by age 12 the prosthetic arm is 4.0 cm shorter than the other arm, and the child leans the trunk about 5° to reach the same things.

**Why.** The prosthesis length was matched to the intact arm on fitting day. The intact forearm keeps growing; the prosthesis does not. The difference is a reach deficit δ, which the child makes up by leaning forward:

\\beta = \\arcsin\\!\\left(\\frac{\\delta}{\\ell_{trunk}}\\right)

Leaning adds a moment at the lower back (the L5/S1 joint) from the weight of the head, arms and trunk.

| Age | Reach deficit | Trunk lean | Extra lower-back moment |
| --- | ------------- | ---------- | ----------------------- |
| 9   | 1.1 cm        | 1.6°       | 0.34 % BW·H             |
| 10  | 2.1 cm        | 3.0°       | 0.64 % BW·H             |
| 11  | 3.0 cm        | 4.2°       | 0.90 % BW·H             |
| 12  | 4.0 cm        | 5.3°       | 1.14 % BW·H             |

**Joint effort.** We divide each joint torque by the child's strength, which grows as M^(2/3)·H (muscle cross-section times lever arm). As the child grows, the prosthetic-side elbow works less (relative to its strength) than the intact elbow, because the prosthesis stays the same size. That could mean that arm is under-used, but it is a model result, not something we measured.

**Say it carefully.** These are trends to watch, not injury predictions. Replacing the socket on schedule keeps the deficit under 2 cm.

**Picture for the video:** fig12_musculoskeletal.

## Verification and uncertainty

Most of the mechanical results are checked by automated tests, and 400 random parameter sets show which uncertain inputs matter most.

**Verification (31 tests, all pass):**

| Check                                              | Result                 |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Arm swinging freely conserves energy               | drift 1×10⁻¹¹ over 3 s |
| Lagrange elbow torque = Newton–Euler moment        | difference 4×10⁻¹⁶ N·m |
| Torques fed back into the ODE reproduce the motion | error 0.007°           |
| Model 1 static hold = Model 0 formula              | exact to 10⁻¹⁰         |
| Growth ODE = closed-form Preece–Baines             | under 10⁻⁶ m           |
| Growth-forced ODE system = algebraic Model 2       | relative 6×10⁻⁸        |
| ODE failure event = direct lifetime search          | within 0.001 months, 28 cases |
| Independent MATLAB code = Python                   | within 0.03 % (re-run matlab/crosscheck.m and confirm this before you say it) |

**Pistoning check.** We also solved an ODE for the socket sliding on the limb:

m\\,\\ddot{u} + c\\,\\dot{u} + k\\,u = -A(t)

Its natural frequency is about 41 Hz, roughly 40 times faster than lifting, and the slip is only 0.28 mm. That justifies treating the socket as quasi-static. (This check is a script, not one of the 31 tests.)

**Uncertainty.**

- **One at a time (±25 %):** movement speed, residual-limb length and radius, and the pressure tolerance matter most. Each of those four pushes a socket fitted at 8 to failure on fitting day when it is changed by 25 % the wrong way, so our baseline sits fairly close to the tolerance. A 25 % shorter residual limb, for example, fails on fitting day.
- **400 Latin-hypercube samples:** a patient-specific fit raises median lifetime from 17.5 to 21.1 months. In 24 % of samples the fast curl is unsafe from day one: for those children the speed of the action, not growth, is the risk.
- **A practical protocol:** the stress index measured on fitting day predicts how long the socket lasts (Spearman ρ = −0.78). Measure socket pressure during a brisk lift at fitting, then let the model schedule the next review.
- Residual-limb length is the strongest driver of the closure age (rank correlation 0.75). The closure age itself is spread widely: 14 % of samples were already closed at age 4, and 33 % never closed before 18.

**Pictures for the video:** fig13_verification, fig10_tornado, fig11_monte_carlo.

## Second pass: making the headline answer robust

**1. A lifetime that doesn't need the tolerance (fig16).** Nobody has measured how much pressure a child's residual limb tolerates, and the lifetime moves a lot with it (80 kPa → 6 months, 100 → 21.6, 120 → 29.5 for a boy fitted at 8). But the *path* of peak pressure P(t) in a frozen socket doesn't depend on the tolerance at all. The socket fails when P(t) reaches the tolerance, so lifetime = time for P to rise by the headroom x = p_tol/P(0) − 1. For a boy fitted at 8, P(0) = 76.7 kPa and P is +10 %, +25 %, +50 % after 11, 19, 28 months (cylindrical). Across ages 6–12, both sexes and both sockets, +25 % comes after 11–26 months. Protocol: measure P(0) at fitting, compare with the clinician's limit, book the review from the path.

**2. Model 2 as differential equations (fig18).** The arm moves in half a second; the socket lasts two years (ratio 9×10⁻⁹). So the arm is the fast subsystem and only its peak load enters the slow one:

- dH/dt = s(t)(h₁ − H) (growth), dℓ/dt = φ f_f dH/dt (limb length)
- dr/dt = ½ r (Ṁ/M − Ḣ/H) (girth), dε/dt = (1/β − ε) ṙ/r (tissue strain), dp/dt = (E + Bp) dε/dt (fit pressure)

The socket's life ends at the first **event**: fit pressure + lifting pressure = tolerance, or friction can no longer hold it on. The solver finds the event by root-finding. It matches the original search to 0.001 months in 28 cases.

**A conserved quantity.** (1 − βε) r stays constant, so the squeeze depends only on how much the girth has grown. A socket has a **girth budget**: with a 5 % fit it is used up after only 5–7 % of girth growth. Girth grows about 3.5 % a year, so lifetime ≈ ln(budget)/rate ≈ 17–22 months. It's girth, not length, that ends the socket.

**3. Closure as a probability (fig17).** 600 random scenarios (tissue values, tolerance, limb size, object share 1–3 % of body mass, and κ, how movement time scales with size). Two readings of residual-limb growth: "as assumed" (45 % of forearm at every fitting) and "self-consistent" (it grows by our rule after age 6). Closure before 18: 58 % and 88 %. Median closure age: 14.3 and 9.9 years. With a load of 1–1.5 % of body mass only 21–57 % close; with 2.5–3 %, 91–100 %. **Say it this way:** closure is a condition to screen for (big everyday loads, short residual limb), not an age.

**4. Validation against published data (fig19, paper Section 11).**

| What | Model | Published | Honest reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Replacement interval | median 17.5 months | 16.4 ± 9.9 months, 62 Cambodian casefiles (Ghidini 2025) | agrees, but this tunes one number (tolerance) and the data are lower-limb |
| Tolerance | 100 kPa (implied 91–99) | children's pain threshold 183 ± 91 kPa (Nikolajsen 2011) | 18th percentile; plausible, not a test |
| Interface pressure | 37–77 kPa | about 40 kPa in adult transhumeral sockets (Razak 2014) | same order of magnitude |
| Girth growth 6→17 | +44 % boys | arm +39 %, wrist +29 % (Öztürk 2009, 2017) | model a little high, so lifetimes a little short |
| Growth-plate share | φ = 0.25 | 5–20 % (Pritchett 1991) | slightly optimistic; φ = 0.10 gives 20.0 instead of 21.6 months |
| Growth ODE | 0.28 cm in-sample | 1.9–6.4 cm out-of-sample | describes the curve, does not predict it |

## Questions judges may ask

Practise these out loud; each answer should take under 20 seconds.

1. **Why is the pressure distribution linear along the socket?** It is the simplest distribution that satisfies both force and moment balance, and it is the classic assumption for a short beam pressed into a soft foundation. A finite-element socket would refine it; the scaling with 1/L² would stay.
2. **Where do the tissue stiffness and tolerance values come from?** They are working assumptions in a plausible range, not measurements on children's arms. That is why we ran the sensitivity and Monte Carlo analyses, and why we propose measuring pressure at fitting. The closure age in particular moves a lot when we change them.
3. **Why does a bigger child reach window closure earlier?** Objects scale with body mass, so the object term rises as the square root of M/H. Heavier-for-height children have larger M/H, so they hit the tolerance sooner.
4. **Why does the limb grow in girth but hardly in length?** About 80–85 % of forearm length growth comes from the growth plates at the wrist end, which a transradial limb lacks. Girth grows with body mass everywhere.
5. **Is assuming loads of 2 % of body mass realistic?** It is a scenario, not a measurement: about 0.5 kg at age 8 and 1 kg at 14. With a fixed 0.5 kg object the window never closes, so we present both and flag the growing-load case as the one needing scrutiny. The result is sensitive to it: at 1.5 % there is no closure before 18, and at 2.5 % it comes at about 10 years.
6. **How do you know the code is right?** Energy is conserved to 10⁻¹¹, two independent formulations agree to 10⁻¹⁶, the dynamic model reduces exactly to our hand-solved Model 0, and a separate MATLAB implementation reproduces the Python results (only say this once you have run crosscheck.m and it agrees).
7. **What would you do with more time?** Calibrate tissue values with pressure-sensor data, use child-specific body proportions, model the 3D tapered socket with finite elements, and add bone overgrowth of the residual limb.
8. **Did you use AI?** Yes, throughout. Our AI Use Report lists the tools, the prompts and what each one did. We checked the equations and results ourselves and with the automated tests.
9. **How sure are you about age 14?** Not very. We tested it: a heavier object, a lower tolerance or a limb that follows our own growth rule all bring it forward by 2 to 7 years, and a lighter object or higher tolerance pushes it past 18. The mechanism is solid; the number isn't.
10. **Why doesn't your straight line for Π pass through 1 at Π = 0?** It is a fit to all 96 runs. Slow curls sit at exactly 1, so the real curve is flat and then rises. We use the line for Π above about 1.

**Q: Isn't 100 kPa just made up?** It is an assumption, which is why our main routine-replacement result is the pressure path, which doesn't use it. For what it's worth, the tolerance that reproduces the clinic mean is 91–99 kPa, at the 15th–18th percentile of children's pain thresholds.

**Q: Where is the differential equation?** Growth (Preece–Baines), the arm (Lagrange), the pistoning check, and the slow growth–load system in which the socket's life ends at a solver event. The conserved quantity (1 − βε)r gives the girth budget in closed form.

**Q: Did you validate it?** Partly. We found no child interface-pressure data, so we compare the pieces around it: replacement intervals, pain thresholds, adult socket pressures, arm and wrist growth, growth-plate shares. We say which comparisons tune a parameter and which are lower-limb.
